Mined from 17 distinct videos (~421K chars) pulled 2026-06-06 — Henri Pierre-Jacques, Brandon Bryant, Jarrid Tingle & team (Harlem Capital Partners; thesis: back 1,000 diverse founders over 20 years), plus carry/2-and-20 explainers. Summarized in own words + brief attributed quotes — not reproductions. This is the investor / capital-allocator layer — the mirror of the founder-side entrepreneurship operator playbook. Maps to Course 10 (Entrepreneurship & Venture) and the capital-allocation thread in canon bezos shareholder letters / canon jensen meckling agency theory.

See also: primary venture partners insights (the scaled-seed counterpart, with a side-by-side table) and apply wss to venture (how rates, credit, the IPO window and the distribution drought reach both firms).

1 · Fund economics — the bedrock mechanics

  • 2-and-20: ~2% annual management fee (a $500M fund → $10M/yr for salaries/offices/diligence) + 20% carried interest = the GP's cut of profits (elite funds 30%; challengers waive/taper the fee).
  • The 4-step distribution waterfall: (1) return of capital to LPs, (2) 8% preferred return / hurdle, (3) GP catch-up, (4) 80/20 split above. Example: $100M fund returns $300M → return $100M → $200M profit → GP carry = $40M.
  • European vs American waterfall: VC uses European (LPs get all capital back first, then 80/20) — because VC loses half+ the portfolio, LPs won't let the GP take carry on the first winner. PE uses American (deal-by-deal carry, with clawbacks if later losses shortchange LPs).
  • Carry is split into units, set up front, and is $0 if the fund never reaches full-carry mode — and then you likely can't raise the next fund. The J-curve + power law (~75% of startups fail) mean winners must cover all losses and return profit; markups are only leading indicators (can evaporate 70%).
  • The carry tax fight: capital-gains vs ordinary-income treatment ("carry loophole") — perennial.

2 · Fund size is the master constraint (everything cascades from it)

  • Camp → ownership → reserves → check size all flow from fund size. Three portfolio-construction camps: concentrated (<20 deals), diversified (20–45, the seed average ~28 per Sapphire), spray-and-pray (45+).
  • Ownership is math indexed to fund size: sub-$50M funds can run low ownership (5–8%) because a $500M–$1B outcome returns the fund; at $100M+ you must own 10–20% or the math fails. HC: "$1–2.5M for 10–15%" — can't go below that threshold. First US funds average $40–50M (the 5–8%-ownership sweet spot).
  • Price only matters relative to fund size (echoes Keith Rabois "seed price doesn't matter" — true only when small). "Markets always correct" — outsized-outcome arguments collapse when valuations drop 70%.
  • Reserves/SPVs are a capacity question, not a right/wrong — how many boards a human can sit on, back-office load. Back into max check: camp → ownership target → reserve model (~1:1) → solve for check.

3 · The two jobs of VC (different skill sets)

  • (1) Pick/win deals vs. (2) run the fund/firm (from TPG's Jim Coulter). Great sourcing makes a great angel; great fund-management is a separate money-management skill (a16z's $4.5B fund ≠ deal-picking). "Minimize headcount, maximize AUM." Emerging managers wrongly think picking = managing.
  • LPs buy institutionalized process, not a lucky home run — they'd take a steady 2x ×10 funds over a 5x-1x-3x-2x scatter. They invest in repeatable sourcing + memos + back-office. "Can you operate at scale for long periods?"
  • Deal memos = 30–60 pages, built in PowerPoint (deals close in 48–72h): consolidate diligence for fast partner review, prove process to LPs, and gift the memo to the founder post-close (+ share downstream to short-circuit the next investor's diligence). Founders are stunned — it shows their flaws and that "we invested" ≠ "we think you're flawless; the reward simply exceeded the risk."
  • Junior-speaks-first IC (associate → GP) + comments in Word not Google Docs, so seniors don't anchor.

4 · How VCs decide — the investment bar

  • HC's box (need 2 of 4 great): Founder, Market, Business, Ownership. Two great → invest; you never get all four. "You don't know a 1-in-1,000 company until you've seen 1,000" — reps compound judgment.
  • The lens shifts with reps + the cycle: deal #1 was an unknown accelerator founder; #50 was someone known 12 years → network-driven, and market now matters far more ("great founder + great company" isn't enough without market tailwind + large TAM). Downturn → away from consumer, toward B2B/vertical software + AI.
  • "Is it venture?" three tests (John Henry): market size; founder vision/storytelling (the swing factor — Casper/SoulCycle/WeWork "weren't obviously venture" but executed that way); will investors actually fund it (Amazon unprofitable for ~decades but fundable). Venture = trade equity for 50%+–3x annual growth and a mandatory IPO/acquisition exit; a 10–15%/yr business is a great company but not venture. (↔ entrepreneurship-playbook §5 "don't put jet fuel in a Camry.")
  • Founder signals others use: Founders Fund — must be the founder's life's work (not a "whiteboard founder"). a16z — the "idea maze" (do they know which turns lead to death vs treasure, who the past casualties were, which tech moves the maze walls?); if stumped in 20 min, bad sign. GV — back velocity (direction + speed), build-for-yourself intuition; joy/delight drives adoption more than productivity.
  • HC's early risk-reduction model: diverse founders often build $100M–$500M companies, so early on HC didn't invest pre-revenue (preferred ~2 yrs of revenue) — the model doesn't require every bet to be a unicorn. Macro: 60% of exits are enterprise but 60% of exit value is consumer (the giant outcomes skew consumer). West Coast = spray-and-pray for billion-dollar swings; East Coast = "intelligent investor" risk-reduction temperament.

5 · Building a fund from nothing (the founder-of-a-fund playbook)

  • The 4 things LPs buy, ranked (Brandon Bryant): (1) Team (who, tenure together, track record — HC met 16 yrs ago, interned/roomed/banked, group-text → LLC; don't raise solo if avoidable). (2) Strategy (stage/asset class + why you are uniquely qualified; research what the LP needs to add to their book). (3) Deals & Sourcing (could be #1 — you need an angel portfolio; LPs reference-call every founder; sourcing is the future bet). (4) Returns (take 10–12 yrs → least important for Fund I, critical by II–III; markups as leading indicators).
  • Start as an angel syndicate: HC began 2015 as an LLC, 4 partners × $5k/deal → one $25k "Harlem Capital Angel" check ("buying businesses instead of bottles" on IB salaries) — one entity converts better than four small checks. Built a track record → institutional Fund I.
  • Fund I was brutal: 18 months, ~400–500 meetings, 12 of 18 months while at HBS (Amtrak to NYC Wed→Sun, fundraised through spring break); 55 LPs, 6 institutions (rare for a first-timer). Fund II: $134M in 6 months (post-George-Floyd tailwind). Took zero salary while raising to avoid "funding their lifestyle with fees." Check size scaled $25k angel → $250k Fund-I-first (a terrifying 10x) → $2M Fund-II-average in ~3 years — it gets easier.
  • GP commit mechanics: standard 1% (HC set it on the target not the cap); Fund II used an SVB GP credit line (bank funds 60% of the stake, GP puts 40% cash) because stacked commitments with no realized carry strain a young GP. "Use other people's money as much as possible" (Henry Kravis was an LP).
  • Most common LP "no": don't back first-timers; don't believe diversity is an asset class; "you can't be a specialist for 30–40% of the market." HC reframe: "we know the underserved 2% better than anyone."
  • Fundraising discipline: ask for the money, not advice ("advice is cheap" — a billionaire's note); do the LP-intro homework for them (scrape the boards your LPs sit on, hand them 5–10 names, ask for 2–3 intros — "it's not my job to find people in your network"); rising minimums ($100k→$250k→$500k) force first-movers; an anchor who advocates (TPG rode along to vouch; sourced 3 of 6 institutions) is worth multiples of its check. "Don't take the no personally — the people you expect to back you won't."
  • The intern engine as moat + mission multiplier: 6 interns × 3 classes/yr; applications 125 → 1,250; 24 alumni now work at other VC funds — seeding diverse investors industry-wide to hit the 1,000-founder goal HC alone (8–15 deals/yr) can't.

6 · Brand / media / trust as the scalable lever

  • Naval's leverage, applied to a small seed fund: capital and headcount don't scale — code and media do — so HC goes all-in on media as its sourcing and capital engine. "You don't have to create, you just document" the journey (wins and losses). "Purpose opens doors profit can't."
  • Brand → inbound, at every scale: "people banged down our doors at $25k checks"; ~$50M of LP capital traced to LinkedIn DMs + press. One Stanford-MBA DM → KKR's Roberts family → first $1M check → TPG anchor → ~$21M direct + halo. A Sunday WSJ print feature → Jamie Dimon's chief of staff emailed within days; two billionaires invested after a CNBC hit. Founders now DM "I've been watching your YouTube" — that is sourcing.
  • Platform discipline: curate LinkedIn for the premium audience (bosses/LPs/founders follow there); diversify platforms (you can lose a channel — post-Elon, X reach collapsed vs LinkedIn). Newsletter/YouTube as owned platforms. Time portfolio press to when product/waitlist can convert, or right before a raise to harvest investor inbound.
  • Trust is the real moat (pre-fundraise): "the future of investing is trust" — when everyone has money and AI to reach founders, the winner is whoever the founder trusts enough to let on the board. So track founders for years before they have a company (ex-OpenAI/Anthropic founding engineers — many 2024–25 $100M–$1B seed rounds went to them); be the first call at company formation. The SoHo HQ (incubate a billion-dollar company in-house, "turn overhead into an asset"), dinners, paddle, basketball are all relationship/sourcing surface. "Maximize your surface area for luck."

7 · The diverse-founder thesis (pitched as inefficiency, not charity)

  • ~3% of VC goes to women/underrepresented founders who are ~70%+ of the population → a market inefficiency → invest in an overlooked group for outsized returns + impact. Funding ebbs/flows with news cycles (spikes post-George-Floyd, #MeToo) → invest counter-cyclically.
  • Two-sided market: capital scales in weeks (OpenAI $40B→$100B) but you must create diverse founders (give them confidence to leave Facebook) — the slow side. "You can't be what you can't see" forces ecosystem/media/events/reports a white-male-Stanford fund never needs ("they can put a sign on the corner and find them"). A diverse GP investing in diverse founders has deeper network effects than a diverse GP with a white portfolio. "Talent is evenly distributed; opportunity is not."
  • Downstream-capital risk is the killer in a downturn (Henri, post-SVB): early-stage isn't immediately hurt, but harder GP fundraising → harder downstream rounds for portfolio cos. HC did zero deals in one Q4 (a first). Post-crash vintages historically outperform; 2021–22 vintages won't.

Founder-side takeaways (the mirror — what to do differently knowing how VCs think)

  1. Know if you're even a venture business — a path to $100M–$1B+ via IPO/acquisition + 50%+ annual growth. If you're a great cash-flow business, a "no" isn't an insult. (↔ playbook §5.)
  2. Match your raise to the investor's fund size — a tiny check from a big fund (or asking a small fund to lead a hot priced round) breaks their ownership math. Understand their portfolio construction first.
  3. Engineer warm intros and do the work for them — pre-build the target list, ask for 2–3 specific intros; the DM that became $21M proves warm + inbound beats spray (~2% cold-reply). (↔ playbook §4.)
  4. Ask for the check, not advice; project calculated conviction.
  5. Storytelling + materials are the gate past ~$3M revenue — investors see 4–5k cos/yr, pick 2–3; have a tight framework, painkiller-not-vitamin clarity, idea-maze depth. (↔ playbook §1 "interesting = no.")
  6. Treat the raise as a distinct, time-boxed job (3–6 months + ~8 weeks of data-room prep); switch from "sell customers" mode to "sell the vision" mode.
  7. Build cash-efficiency / a clear milestone in — don't assume a quick markup round (the 2021 fallacy); downstream-capital risk can strand you. (↔ playbook §5 "between-rounds death.")
  8. Win on more than money — at 10 term sheets, pick the investor with unique value-add/network/trust; and remember your investor still prices real risk in you (the memo proves it).
  9. Use brand strategically but authentically ("document, don't create"); time announcements to convert the funnel. "You're always launching" — give each pivot a real 90-day–6-month test, then kill fast.

Cross-cutting (vs. the canon & the founder playbook)

  • Same decision, two seats. Dilution/ownership, "is it venture," PMF, distribution-as-moat all appear in entrepreneurship operator playbook from the founder's seat and here from the allocator's — reading both gives the full table, which is the "advise executives / understand the landscape" muscle.
  • Capital allocation is the throughline to the canon — carry/waterfall/power-law economics are canon jensen meckling agency theory (GP/LP incentives) + canon bezos shareholder letters (returns on invested capital) in practitioner language. Brand-as-distribution echoes the playbook's "distribution is the new moat."

Batch 2 — Mined from 10 additional videos (~485K chars) pulled 2026-09-09. Speakers: Brandon Bryant, Henri Pierre-Jacques, Nihal Mehta (Eniac), Ben Lerer (Lerer Hippeau), Ben Sun (Primary VC), Beezer Clarkson (Sapphire Partners / CalSTRS), Charles (Rain), Nicole Wisoff (HC), Dorm Room Fund principals. These deepen prior sections and add new dimensions: the LP seat, scaled seed economics, AI-as-operational-infrastructure, the NYC ecosystem thesis, and second-time founder mechanics.

8 · Brandon's 4-characteristic framework (deepening §4)

  • 5,000 deals/year, invests in <10 → 99%+ rejection rate. The four things that convince an investor to write the check: 1. Management Team — broken into four sub-tests: (a) Tenure — prefer teams that have worked together at multiple companies or known each other for years (college roommates, childhood teammates). High-stakes + money strains relationships; prior trust provides resilience. (b) Experience / Expertise — domain fit. AI agents for dental practices? Want someone who went to dental school, family managed 30 practices, or manufactured dental products. Not transferable skills — actual domain lineage. (c) Pedigree / Reputation — not just school logos but "best professor at best dental school would say you were a top student." Three-question reference protocol: (1) Are they exceptional to work with? (2) Would you invest your own personal capital? (3) Would you start a business with them? All three yeses → go deeper on superpowers. (d) Culture / Mission — what type of people does this company attract? "OpenAI people vs Anthropic people vs Brex people vs Ramp people are all different types." The mission shapes the talent pool and therefore the execution ceiling. 2. Velocity — not raw speed but how fast you get to the right solution. "Good businesses don't avoid problems — they solve problems faster than other businesses." Lean into adversity, not away from it. "Anyone can start an app now with AI — the question is how fast you get to the product that runs someone's entire business." (Echoes entrepreneurship operator playbook §5 PMF velocity.) 3. Ability to hire exceptional talent — can you recruit from centers of excellence? (nuclear company pulling engineers from SpaceX, NASA, Anduril, Uber Freight, Tesla). Can you retain them? What is your reputation around talent? "A+ players want to play with other A+ players — LeBron's team, not a no-name's team." (↔ canon bezos shareholder letters "hire missionaries not mercenaries.") 4. Intangibles / Superpowers — irreplicable founder qualities. Sierra's Bret Taylor: started company acquired by Facebook, CTO of Facebook mid-20s, chairman of Twitter, co-CEO Salesforce, now chairman of OpenAI. That access/insight creates 10x–1000x leverage. Pattern: founders who sold sneakers on the internet as teenagers (Cursor founders, MerchCore founders, Brandon himself — eBay power seller at 16). "Can you productize that unfair advantage?"
  • Ownership math reiterated: 5% of a $1B exit vs 8% = difference between 5x-ing and 8x-ing the fund. "Every single piece of ownership from your first investment is very important." (Reinforces §2.)

9 · Henri's IC mechanics and voting system (deepening §3 & §4)

  • 1-to-10 scoring system: every partner scores each deal. Average deal score across the portfolio: 7.6; top-performing investments averaged 8.1–8.2. The delta looks tiny but is statistically significant across hundreds of deals.
  • Single-partner conviction cap: 60% of deals. Maximum fraction of investments where only one partner has high conviction — the rest must have broader team buy-in. Team vote correlates more strongly with outcome than any individual partner's enthusiasm.
  • Speed metrics: fastest deal ever closed in 36 hours; average from first call to term sheet: 13 days.
  • Four founder archetypes that HC sorts into: (1) Stars (obvious talent, pedigree, momentum), (2) Veterans (deep industry operators who know the space cold), (3) Academics (researchers with technical depth turning insights into products), (4) Operators (execution machines from scaled companies). Each archetype has different risk profiles and evaluation heuristics.
  • Diversification across 10 dimensions — not just sector/stage but geography, founder background, business model, customer segment, etc. Deliberate portfolio balance; no single dimension dominates. Josh Kaufman ownership target: think backwards from "what ownership % do I need at exit to return the fund?"
  • References beat interviews (Harvard Business School study Henri cites) — what former colleagues say predicts founder success better than any interview performance. HC operationalizes this: reference calls on every founder, not just competitive deals.
  • Fund I median ownership: 8%; Fund II: 10%. The step-up tracks fund-size scaling (§2) — larger fund demands more ownership, which demands larger checks, which demands winning competitive rounds.
  • 100 interns through the program, 34 now work in venture — evolving the metric from §5's earlier count. HC's intern engine is now producing a measurable fraction of diverse VCs industry-wide.

10 · The LP perspective — what allocators actually want (Beezer Clarkson / Sapphire Partners)

  • Sapphire Partners + CalSTRS partnership: Sapphire acquired CalSTRS's legacy emerging-manager VC portfolio and the go-forward program. CalSTRS = world's largest educator pension. "We feel immense gratitude and responsibility investing teachers' pensions" — changes the LP's risk tolerance calculus. CalSTRS has been investing in emerging managers (both PE and VC) since the early 2000s — decades of institutional commitment. (↔ canon jensen meckling agency theory — principal monitors agent.)
  • The universal filter — same for emerging and established managers:
  • Seed/pre-seed funds → can this be a 5x net?
  • Series A funds → can this be a 3x net?
  • Later stage → same math, just harder to see a $3B vehicle at 3x. This is why Sapphire focuses where they focus: return potential ceiling drives allocation.
  • Fund 1 data gap: LP must infer from prior career. What has the GP done that gives reason to believe they can be this kind of investor? Fund 2–3 → more data: portfolio selection, go-to-market, how they compete, firm structure. "Same filter, different inputs."
  • Deck requirements (what to include when pitching an LP):
  • Team as people, not logos — who you are, not just where you went to school.
  • Have you managed someone else's money? Even at scout/AngelList level. Sapphire has not yet invested in someone who has never managed external capital. (Tension with §5's "start from zero" playbook — there's a gap between angel-with-own-money and LP-ready.)
  • Check sizes + portfolio construction alignment — $5–10K checks before ≠ $1M checks now requires translation. $200K→$200K is an easier narrative than $5K→$1M.
  • The "why you" factor — not just the thesis but why this GP is the best person on the planet to execute it. What network, access, or insight creates a right to win?
  • Loom video over a deck = "amazing" — 3 minutes of talking points over slides. One-to-many format that lets the LP process asynchronously. Beezer: "if I could wave a magic wand and have that happen always, it was just the best."
  • Audited funds required at institutional LP level (vs. sub-$10M friends-and-family funds that don't need audits). This is a structural gate between angel-fund and institutional-fund worlds.
  • Portfolio construction: open-minded but guarded. Generalist, specialist, concentrated, diversified — all can work. But: "if you want a billion-dollar fund with 1% stake in 2,000 companies, the math is going to work against you." Many emerging managers lack experience to model their own portfolio outcomes. An LP like Sapphire thinks in portfolio-outcome distributions; the GP should too.
  • First-principles thinking separates winners: "The people I see being successful really sit down and think through what they believe is true about themselves as investors, what they believe about the world, how they do this." Authentic + unique perspective is "really powerful."
  • Venture's time horizon is extreme: each fund vehicle = 15–18–20 years. "Longer than marriages. Your kid's not going to be at home that long." If you're not committed for 40+ years of fund-raising cycles, consider alternatives: AngelList, rolling funds, scouts. "Raising for institutional LPs might not be the best way to dabble." (Counterpoint to the "anyone can start a fund" narrative.)
  • Current market advice (2025–26):
  • Harder market — don't sugarcoat it. Valuations "all over the place."
  • Communicate portfolio development at a granular level: not just TVPI but product-market fit, growth rates, cash burn, operating margin. LPs are asking for operational insight, not just marks.
  • "The last few years were an aberration, not the norm." Fundraising taking longer is historically normal.
  • Some EMs merging with others or hanging up skates — "fine too."
  • "When the good times come back, we'll know what to do."
  • Beezer's own first fund shut down: "going through down markets teaches you a ton."
  • Social media / brand for EMs (LP view): Sapphire is not opposed — wants to understand how it supports strategy. If it increases sourcing, builds community, opens doors → great. If it's a disproportionate time sink that's "fun but not productive" → that's a flag. Old analogy: "how many hours a day are you spending golfing, Mr. VC?" Build-in-public and rolling-fund fundraising via social media: "phenomenal" — funds that couldn't have existed through traditional channels have been raised this way.
  • Open LP democratization thesis: "The arbitrage shouldn't be that Nicole knows how to make a data room better than Beezer — that's a crappy competitive advantage." The same way founders shouldn't fail because they didn't know interview structure, GPs shouldn't fail because they didn't know how LPs think. "It's hard enough to pick great companies — the other stuff should be table stakes."

11 · Emerging-manager scaling playbook (Eniac $1.6M→$220M, Primary $60M→$1.65B)

Eniac (Nihal Mehta)

  • Fund I: $1.6M (2009). No fees taken — fees would have been ~$30K/year ("can't pay anyone off that"). Three founding partners are all engineers, still running startups — investing was "nights and weekends, an experiment." Treated it like a real fund: 32–40 slugs per fund, half reserved for follow-on — same portfolio construction since inception.
  • Transition: "when you can pay yourself from your hobbies, you're living the dream." Nights-and-weekends became the day job.
  • Current state (Fund VII, $220M): 4 partners (Tim, Hadley, Kristen, Nihal), steady state of ~10 people + 1 junior investor + platform + CFO + ops. Lean and partner-centric even at $220M. (↔ §2 "minimize headcount, maximize AUM.")
  • The seed investor landscape has leveled: "if you look at the seed investors of all the AI unicorns and decacorns, there's not actually one consistent seed investor. They're young, older, second-time, all over the place. It gets consolidated downstream [Series A/B/C] at Andreessen, Thrive, Lightspeed, Sequoia." The implication: seed is democratized, Series A+ is oligopolistic.
  • The Human Rolodex method: old-school Google Sheet with tabs by city, always open on every machine, 20+ years running. People at top of each list = need to catch up with. When visiting a city, "bomb that list." "Karma is real in our industry — when you help a bunch of folks, it comes back 100x." Ahimsa philosophy (Jain principle of non-violence/compassion): give without asking for anything in return. "Reputation compounds over years — it can be broken in a second." (↔ §6 trust-as-moat.)
  • Pitch and Run: running community for founders, now in 18 cities. Monday circle: introduce yourself, put something you want to manifest for the week. "Building a startup is very lonely — other founders know." Organic exponential growth over 5 years. (Relationship/sourcing surface — extends §6.)

Primary VC (Ben Sun)

  • Origin story: Ben Sun founded Community Connect (AsianAvenue/BlackPlanet/MiGente) — 12-year run. First VC investor was Bob Goldhammer, early 70s, former Kidder Peabody vice chairman, didn't use email ("I had to fax him everything"). Bob invested $5M and said: "more importantly, I'm betting on you." Bob's prior bet: a biotech penny stock (the Waxel brothers) → sold to Eli Lilly for $7B. Lesson: "the amazing thing about people is they could have potentially unlimited upside."
  • Post-exit reflection: "Were my VCs really that helpful beyond the capital? No." Plus some "shady maneuvering" — VCs agreeing to terms then trying to change at the last minute. Bob (not a VC) was the real mentor. This shaped Primary's north star: "the more you operationally get involved and know the ground truth, the better the investor you'll be. Over time, if you build a reputation of being really helpful, you get the better deals with the best founders."
  • Angel period / Coupang: invested own capital for 4–5 years. Met Bomb Kim playing pickup basketball at Stuyvesant High School. Brainstormed ideas for a year (none stuck). Bomb went to HBS; over lunch Ben explained Groupon → Bomb said "will this work for Korea?" → dropped out of HBS → Ben invested + joined board. Coupang is now a $40–50B market cap, 100K+ employees, the Amazon + DoorDash of Korea. Ben put together SPVs totaling ~$50M invested → over $1B in returns at IPO. "Life-changing event."
  • Meeting co-founder Brad: Brad had started High Peaks (a fund where his two partners lost 95 cents on the dollar, but Brad carried it to a 1.5x fund). LPs bet on Brad solo → he raised a second fund but hated being a solo GP ("a really lonely job"). 2.5-hour lunch → co-founded Primary in 2013–14.
  • NYC thesis (2013–14): "Tumblr ($1B to Yahoo) was the biggest exit in NYC tech history. We had one unicorn exit." Thesis: New York was always a great magnet for talent — they just weren't working on startups. Financial crisis displaced 200K Wall Street jobs → Mark Lori (Diapers.com/Jet/Wonder), Dave Gilboa (Warby Parker), Alexa von Tobel (LearnVest), etc. "Talent was there; opportunity wasn't."
  • Fund I–II ($60M + $100M, NYC-only): 8 unicorns from ~35 deals — an extraordinary hit rate. Then the secret got out: 50+ NYC tech IPOs (Datadog, MongoDB, Oscar, Peloton, Warby Parker, DoubleVerify, Yext...), 150 private unicorns (#2 after Bay Area, more than next 10 markets combined). Every VC opened a NYC office. "Who's your competition? Everybody."
  • Scaling into industrialized seed: US seed market grew from ~$5B to $20B+ in 10 years (4x). Millions of people now work at venture-backed companies → primordial pool of founding talent → AI as the spark. Capital follows great people on great ideas. A $1B seed fund deploying $200M/year in checks = 1% of the seed market. The framing resets the "too big for seed" objection.
  • Management fees as the operating budget: 2% of a bigger fund → bigger team → more surface area. Primary now: 65+ people (growing to 80), 10 recruiters who directly placed 170 people in portfolio companies last year. Go-to-market team. Strategic finance support. "Most seed funds were small boutiquey low-resource firms — we said, how do we supercharge it?"
  • Primary's 4 controllable inputs (borrowed from Amazon's outputs-vs-inputs framework): 1. Seeing deals (events, content marketing, AI sourcing agents). 2. Picking deals (research, intel, team analysis). 3. Winning deals ("forward-deployed motion" — learn the business during diligence, pitch with actual customers found and recruits identified, not just slides). 4. Supporting deals (recruiters, go-to-market, strategic finance embedded in portfolio cos).
  • "Show don't tell" in the win pitch: go-to-market team literally builds a custom app/dashboard for each finalist company showing customers they've already sourced, enriched with AI signals (e.g., combing Google reviews for a home-services AI company to find which merchants are the best prospects). Not slides — a working tool. "When we do it, they're like, wow, this is different."
  • Fund size ≠ worse returns (contrarian): "it's not really the size, it's the stage." Early stage = high return dispersion (one fund 50x, another 0x). Late stage = compressed (3x vs 1.5x). Reporting the "best funds" picks the top of the high-dispersion distribution, which are small because they're early stage, not because small is inherently better. Primary's largest fund is on track to be their best performer. (Important counter-narrative to the conventional "small fund = better returns" heuristic.)
  • Altus (incubation — VC research-as-a-product): Tiger Global paid Bain $100M+/yr to do pre-meeting research on companies (customers, competitors, former employees, other investors). Tiger showed up knowing the company better than the founder knew it. Primary co-founded Altus to democratize this: institutional research on private companies (Harvey, Lora, 11 Labs, plus smaller startups) available to any investor. Pitchbook: acquired at $30M ARR, now does $700M ARR + $400M FCF. The VC research market is large and growing. (Emerging entrepreneurship operator playbook case: research-as-infrastructure for an opaque market.)
  • Steve Jobs priority framework (via Kevin Ryan / DoubleClick): new hire lists 30 priorities → boss tears off all but the top 2. "Focus on these two things, forget everything else." Operationalized at Primary: every investor writes an annual strategic plan — portfolio review, market mapping, competitive landscape, target founders, target sectors. Measurable KPIs (deals seen, win rate). "You can't do strategic thinking well unless you can measure the results."

12 · AI as operational infrastructure for VCs

  • Eniac (all-Claude shop): Affinity + Gmail + GCal + AirTable → all integrated with Claude. Inbound emails are summarized and posted to a Slack #new-deals channel instantly. System is learning to tag specific partners by sector. Next: read Slack responses and auto-connect founders with interested partners.
  • Eniac's AI-powered diligence: before sending a term sheet, Nihal had Claude read: entire Slack deal channel, all emails + references, all CircleBack audio/video call transcripts (including meetings he wasn't in), the pitch deck + space research. IC had ~20 open questions → Claude scanned first-party data and "went on the internet" → answered them with green check marks by morning, flagged 2–3 for manual follow-up. "My agent says do the deal." Term sheet went out Friday. (Validates canon bezos shareholder letters "high-velocity decision-making" — AI compresses the information-gathering loop without changing the judgment call.)
  • Primary OS (4-person internal AI team): AI sourcing agents comb LinkedIn for signals — who's starting a company, GitHub activity, research papers, math competitions, "or a whole bunch of other VCs are looking at them." Agents reach out, gather information, enrich profiles. Go-to-market team builds per-company customer-sourcing apps with AI enrichment. "You can't afford an AI tooling team unless you have the budget and scale." (Makes the case that scale funds can wield AI as a structural moat over boutique funds.)
  • Lerer Hippeau: "We're a Claude shop. Getting a huge amount of value in a bunch of different places. I want to automate every repetitive workflow we have. It's doing incredible analytical work."
  • Rain (startup side): doesn't prescribe AI tools, sets goals that may require AI to achieve. "I'm going to judge you on the outputs, not on the inputs." Provides whatever AI budget people need + data access + controls. AI-native org → keeps team flat with 25 direct reports (inspired by Jensen Huang's 60 direct reports). (↔ canon bezos shareholder letters two-pizza teams — AI may obsolete the team-size constraint entirely.)

13 · Anti-consensus investing and the "messy middle" (Lerer Hippeau)

  • Ben Lerer's frame: "Venture capital should exist to take risks that most people don't want to take. A lot of VC right now is taking risks that everyone wants to take. That's not risk — that's consensus investing. Consensus investing means you're investing in things that are highly competitive, which means prices are super high. And investing in venture at super high prices is a really shitty business model."
  • "The fun of venture" = be in the generational company that people don't expect, at a price where "when you're right, you're really really really right." Non-consensus + right = outsized returns. Consensus + right = mediocre returns (price paid too high). (↔ Howard Marks: "you can't do the same thing as everyone else and expect to outperform." See canon bezos shareholder letters contrarian bets.)
  • The messy middle: "a lot of money in the ground that's going to zero." Not Open AI / Anthropic money, but the middle tier — companies that raise at higher prices early → "appear more successful" → get marked up faster. But DPI is "really really really really hard." Tiger/SoftBank in '21: some great companies, but that money also "destroyed a lot of companies." In ZIRP bubble, Series C failure rates looked more like seed failure rates — "that screws with the market."
  • AI market specifically: "we have top-tipped the market in this particular moment of AI." Not bearish on Anthropic/AI long-term, but the fervor of daily/weekly mega-rounds into productless, revenue-less neo labs is "on the backside." Next phase: prove it. Application layer is where value accrues, and "that's New York time."
  • The 3-fund hump: every 3 funds, you must demonstrate DPI to raise the next 3. Funds that appear to be the "best thing since sliced bread" often haven't driven much DPI because converting paper returns to real exits is extraordinarily hard. (Critical check on TVPI-as-vanity-metric.)
  • LH's portfolio examples of non-consensus wins:
  • Augmoto: camera name badges tracking retail inventory in real time — "graveyard of companies" tried to sell hardware+software to supermarkets; Sand Hill Road sees the deck and says "next." But exponentially more demand than supply now.
  • Caladan: desktop bioreactors from ground zero — multi-year pre-revenue, large incumbents with long-term relationships. "Years later — yep, they did it." The pattern: hard markets + non-obvious bets + time = outsized returns when it works.

14 · The New York ecosystem thesis

  • Nihal (Eniac): "New York is by far the most ambitious place on the planet." Not concentrated in one industry like SF — density of ambition across law, medicine, modeling, real estate, politics, activism, entrepreneurship. "Every day you can fill your calendar with 12 meetings of people better than you." NYC = horizontal ambition + diversity of experience. SF = concentrated AI depth. "For people looking to build in horizontal environments and have diversity in their lives, New York's the place."
  • Ben Lerer (LH): "If New York sets its sights on anything, it figures it out. Maybe the greatest city in the world, maybe in the history of the world." When LH started, "everybody who was doing VC could fit in this room." Any fund deploying money in NYC saw everything — no competition. Now NYC is huge, but still produces bigger and bigger outcomes.
  • Ben Sun (Primary): Tumblr was the biggest NYC exit in 2015. By 2020–22: 50+ NYC tech IPOs (Datadog, MongoDB, Oscar, Peloton, Warby Parker), 150 private unicorns — more unicorns than the next 10 markets combined (LA + Chicago + Miami's 6 unicorns + etc.). NYC became the #2 global tech market in a few years.
  • AI application layer = NYC's next advantage: foundation models and infrastructure → SF. Application layer (B2C + B2B) → NYC. 9M+ consumers in the tri-state area for consumer apps. Highest concentration of Fortune 500 HQs for enterprise sales ("Jamie Diamond comes to work every day and takes meetings"). AI- native companies "don't need hundreds of folks — you need maybe dozens" → NYC's lifestyle + talent magnet advantage strengthens.
  • Recruiting advantage: Traversal (Columbia professor, backed by Sequoia + Kleiner) says NYC is the best place to recruit — less competition for engineers, and "every young person wants to live in New York."
  • Charles (Rain): SF still #1 for tech broadly, #1 for AI. But SF has "monoculture / group think" — if you're building for the rest of the world, that's a disadvantage. NYC = center of finance + global diversity. "Third wave of NYC startups — there's now enough ecosystem to build successfully here."

15 · Second-time founder mechanics and the idea maze (Rain + DRF)

Rain (Charles)

  • First company → Intuit acquisition: Stanford CS 2012, saved $50K at Microsoft ("if I save 50K, I could squeeze that for a year"), quit. Built contractor management tools, sold to Intuit earlier than expected. Stayed 4.5 years for the learning (beyond the 3-year vest). "Training ground for shipping products and leading teams."
  • The idea maze in practice: "Pick a direction and just make progress. Don't get stuck figuring out where the end of the maze is." Worked on 5 different product ideas. World changed (COVID) → ideas changed. Eventually found co-founder Farooq through Deck Founder Fellowship. Built SignInWire (fundraising doc + payment tool) as a microsaas — "not meant to be venture scale, we just wanted to work together and build something." Through building it, discovered the real problem: broken financial rails.
  • SignInWire → Rain pivot: added USDC to SignInWire → investor in Singapore sent funds on Christmas Day when banks were closed → "aha moment: this is 100x better." But couldn't spend USDC anywhere → the acceptance/interoperability layer became the real business. Led to Visa principal membership (multi-year, "a lot of chewing glass") → world's first 24/7 stable coin settlement → cut out banking dependencies entirely → lower cost of capital + reduced collateral.
  • Stable coin thesis: 1% of M2 money supply is in stable coins today. "If you think money is going to go on-chain and become tokenized and move at the speed of the internet, then 1% is eventually going to be 100%." Timeline uncertain (5/10/20 years) but monotonically increasing.
  • Three rounds in 12 calendar months: "You kind of have to will it into existence." Went to market in 2024 "a little bit prematurely" — had product velocity but too-early revenue for investors to appreciate. Ground out 6 months with a smaller team, proved the revenue, and then "without even trying to fundraise, people were knocking on our door." "No amount of PowerPoint wizardry is going to help — the business has to speak for itself." (↔ §4 — revenue velocity as the ultimate conviction driver.)
  • Second-time founder psychology: advantages = know the emotional roller coaster, willing to play the game again with that assumption. Traps = "you know all the bad things that are going to happen and you're scared to repeat the mistakes" → over-index away from hard things. Consumer was brutal → flee to B2B without knowing how to sell to enterprises. "Starting a startup is about running through walls — you shouldn't be avoiding those moments."
  • HC pattern: 6 investments into second-time founders in 2025. Most of them focused on distribution the second time around — not just brute-force selling but strategic channel leverage (Rain + Visa is the paradigm case).
  • Culture at scale (20→120+ in 12 months): 25 direct reports, inspired by Jensen. Screen for autonomy ("go figure it out"), low ego, no empire-building, high bias toward action. "Don't get stuck in figuring out task-level direction — we set aggressive goals that may not be achievable without AI."

Dorm Room Fund (pre-seed student investing)

  • Structure: Founded 2012 by Josh Koppelman / First Round Capital. 60 student partners, 4 teams of 15, 3% acceptance rate (harder to get into than some VC firms). Went national in 2020. 500+ alumni, 8 unicorns (including second check into Cursor).
  • Information asymmetry edge: students can evaluate student founders better than any institutional VC. They see founders in class, in dorms, on campus — ground truth that no Zoom call or reference check replicates. Pre-seed = maximum information asymmetry advantage. (↔ canon jensen meckling agency theory — information asymmetry creates alpha in private markets.)
  • "No chumps" rule: don't invest in people who cut corners or lack integrity, regardless of traction. Character is the one un-coachable founder attribute.
  • Sneaker reselling as founder signal (also noted in Brandon's intangibles framework): founders who ran reselling businesses as teenagers demonstrate marketplace intuition, hustle, and commercial instinct before they've built anything "official." Pattern appears across Cursor, MerchCore, and multiple DRF-backed founders.
  • DPI focus: student fund emphasizes realized returns, not paper markups. Aligns with Beezer's LP perspective (§10) — "the last few years were an aberration."

16 · HC origin story and firm-building details (deepening §5)

  • December 2015: 5 people (met through MLT — Management Leadership for Tomorrow). Pooled $5K each per deal. Formed a single LLC so one entity could write one check (vs. 5 tiny checks). Adapted a private equity framework (diligence memos, structured IC) to angel investing — unusual rigor at that scale. Transition from 5 to 4 members; later added John Henry.
  • Henri's HBS fundraising cadence (Fund I): Mon–Wed = HBS classes. Thu–Fri = Amtrak to NYC to fundraise. Through spring break. "Took zero salary while raising." First close: $2M (November 2018). Apple LP for $10M — Apple's first-ever VC fund investment. TPG anchor (Jim Coulter rode along to vouch for HC at LP meetings, sourced 3 of 6 institutional LPs). Total Fund I: 55 LPs, 6 institutions.
  • "Not an impact fund — a VC fund with impact." Henri's reframe: impact framing triggers lower-return expectations and concessionary capital. HC wants market-rate returns from an underserved market. The thesis is market inefficiency (§7), not philanthropy.
  • Angel program pipeline: 300 applications → choose 6 angels per cohort. 60 interns → 17 (now 34) placed in VC. "You can't hit 1,000 diverse founders at 8–15 deals/year — you need to seed the ecosystem."

Updated founder-side takeaways (Batch 2 additions)

  1. Will the business into existence through revenue velocity — Rain's three rounds in 12 months happened after proving revenue, not before. "No amount of storytelling or PowerPoint wizardry is going to help" once you pass the seed stage. The business must speak for itself. (Extends takeaway #5.)
  2. Choose distribution over brute force the second time — HC's pattern across 6 second-time-founder bets in 2025: all focused on leveraging existing distribution (Rain + Visa, not building merchant acceptance from scratch). Think about who has already solved the distribution problem and how to partner with them.
  3. Prepare for the LP lens if you're raising a fund — LPs filter on "can this be 3x–5x net?" Seed aspirants must model portfolio outcomes (not just pick companies). Manage others' money first (scout, AngelList, rolling fund). Get audited. Have a 15–20-year commitment horizon. Send a Loom video over your deck.
  4. Your intangibles are leverage — identify and productize them — Brandon's 4th characteristic. What can your team do that nobody else can? Sneaker reselling, chess championships, domain-specific pedigree. Find the 10x–1000x unfair advantage and make it visible in the pitch.
  5. Reference checks > interviews — VCs increasingly weight what former colleagues say over how a founder performs in a pitch meeting. Build a reputation that survives scrutiny when the investor calls your old boss, co-founder, or direct report.
  6. Be non-consensus and right — Lerer Hippeau's frame: consensus investing at high prices is "a really shitty business model." The outsized returns come from companies people don't expect, at prices where being right makes you really right. If every VC wants in, the price already reflects consensus — and the upside is compressed.

Cross-cutting additions (Batch 2)

  • The LP-GP-founder triple alignment: Beezer's LP perspective (§10) adds the third seat at the table. Founders see the VC; VCs see the LP; but most founders never consider LP incentives — preferred returns, DPI obsession, 15–20-year vehicle horizons, the 3-fund hump. Understanding all three seats is the full capital-allocation picture. (↔ canon jensen meckling agency theory — nested principal-agent chains.)
  • AI as the new leverage layer: Naval's leverage taxonomy (§6) was capital, labor, code, media. AI is now a fifth: Eniac's "army of agents" for deal processing, Primary's AI sourcing/customer-finding tools, Rain's AI-native flat org. The firms that build proprietary AI workflows earliest will compound an operational advantage that compounds like brand — hard to replicate, easy to extend. (↔ canon bezos shareholder letters "build on things that won't change" — the underlying principle is information compression, which AI accelerates.)
  • NYC as the application-layer thesis: a cross-source consensus (Eniac, LH, Primary, Rain) that SF owns foundation models but NYC owns the application layer — consumer (9M+ density) and enterprise (Fortune 500 HQ concentration). AI-native companies need dozens, not hundreds → NYC lifestyle + talent magnet advantage strengthens. This is a geographic portfolio construction insight for both LPs and founders choosing where to build.
  • The "industrialized seed" paradigm shift: Primary's $1.65B seed fund, Lerer Hippeau's 9th fund at $1.4B+ AUM, the US seed market at $20B+ — seed is no longer a cottage industry. The implication: seed- stage founders now face institutional-grade investors with AI-powered sourcing, professional win processes ("show don't tell" with custom apps), and portfolio support at a level previously reserved for Series A+. The bar has risen; founders should calibrate expectations accordingly.
  • DPI as the ultimate truth: repeated across Beezer (LP view), Ben Lerer (3-fund hump), Henri (markups ≠ returns), and the Dorm Room Fund (DPI focus). Paper returns are "leading indicators that can evaporate 70%." The entire LP community is recalibrating from TVPI to DPI post-ZIRP. Founders should understand that their investors' fundraising ability — and therefore their own downstream-capital access — depends on realized exits, not markups.
